title: Obedience (ch. 5)

lines: SURE, AND A SPEECH IN HIS HEAD.
THE TRASH GOES OUT. SO DOES A CLOUD.
cards: A teenager is asked to take the trash out. He says sure. He even does it.

But all the way down the driveway a speech runs in his head: why is it always me, nobody else ever does this, I was in the middle of something. The trash makes it to the curb. So does a small gray cloud.
Saint Benedict gives that cloud a name: murmuring. In chapter five he goes after it, because in his Rule the task is only half the matter.

teach.b: Chapter five opens plainly: the first step of humility is obedience without delay. Benedict draws a picture.
A monk is told to do something, and he puts down what's in his hands, unfinished, so that the hearing and the doing happen almost together.

teach.h: HE THAT HEARETH YOU, HEARETH ME.
teach.b: He ties this to words of Jesus in Luke, in the Douay-Rheims: "He that heareth you, heareth me." For Benedict, a word from the abbot is answered as though God were the one asking. Then he raises the bar.

Doing the thing isn't enough. It should be done without hesitating, without dragging the feet, without coldness, without grumbling, and without a reply that shows unwillingness. He means the grumbling inside, too.

teach.h: NOT EVEN MURMURING IN THE HEART.
teach.b: If a monk obeys but murmurs in his heart, God sees the heart, and the work isn't accepted. For the other side he borrows a line from Paul: "God loveth a cheerful giver." The Rule keeps that high bar human in two ways.

teach.h: YOU MAY EXPLAIN. OBEY ONE ANOTHER.
teach.b: In a later chapter, a monk handed something that seems impossible may go to his superior, patiently and at a fitting moment, and explain why. Obedience isn't pretending a heavy load is light.

And near the end of the Rule, Benedict says obedience is a good to be shown not only to the abbot but to one another. So it isn't a chain of command running downhill. It's a whole house leaning toward yes.
Outside a monastery, nobody vows obedience to an abbot, but anyone can notice the speech that runs under a chore, and let it go quiet.

how: Benedictine monks and nuns promise obedience when they make their vows, and the community hears the Rule read aloud, including chapter five on obedience without delay or grumbling.

o: doing every order in silence, even impossible ones
fear of punishment from the abbot above
a ready yes, without grumbling inside or out

s: for Benedict, getting the task done is all that matters
he says a monk who obeys but murmurs in his heart isn't accepted by God, who sees the heart.
the Rule lets a monk explain when a task seems impossible
in a later chapter he may go to his superior, patiently and at a fitting moment, and say why.
in the Rule, obedience runs only from the monk to the abbot
near the end, Benedict says to show obedience to one another, too.

games.q: you're a monk, halfway through copying a page, when you're called to help in the kitchen. what does chapter five ask?
o: finish the page first, then go.
put the pen down, leave the page unfinished, and go.
go, but make sure everyone sees you're annoyed.
games.why: Benedict pictures a monk leaving his work unfinished, so hearing and doing happen almost together, and doing it without grumbling.

practice: Bring to mind one task you'd rather skip today, the dishes, an email, a phone call, and picture starting it.

Listen for the speech that starts up with it, the why me, the not now; don't argue, just let it get quieter on the out-breath, and picture your hands simply doing what hands do. If you pray, offer the task to God before you begin.

wordCard.voice: Obedience. For Benedict, a ready yes, given without delay and without grumbling, out loud or inside. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, the language of the Rule: obedience, the subject of chapter five.

carryVoice: Your line: no murmuring. The task is only half of it; the heart is the other half. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: He that heareth you, heareth me.

sources.ref: Rule of Saint Benedict, ch. 68 and ch. 71
